Abstract Algebra — 04 · Rings, Ideals, Integral Domains and Fields

Created2025-12-01|Updated2025-12-01|Mathematics > Abstract Algebra
|Post View:

Groups have one operation. Most of the algebra you already use has two: integers, polynomials and matrices can be added and multiplied, and the distributive law ties the two together. A structure with both is a ring. This post builds ring theory the same way posts 01–03 built group theory: definitions and examples, then substructures (ideals play the role of normal subgroups), quotients and a First Isomorphism Theorem. Two questions then drive the rest. Which rings behave like Z\mathbb{Z}Z, with unique factorisation? And how do you manufacture new fields, such as C\mathbb{C}C or a field with 4 elements? The answer to the second, "take polynomials modulo an irreducible polynomial", is the starting point of Galois theory in post 05.

Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields (this post) → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory.

Learning Outcome

  • State the ring axioms (with identity), and recognise units, zero divisors, integral domains and fields.
  • Prove that a finite integral domain is a field and that the characteristic of a domain is 0 or a prime.
  • Define ring homomorphisms, ideals and quotient rings, and prove the First Isomorphism Theorem for rings.
  • Prove that R/PR/PR/P is a domain exactly when PPP is prime, and R/MR/MR/M is a field exactly when MMM is maximal.
  • Use the division algorithm in F[x]F[x]F[x] and prove that F[x]F[x]F[x] is a principal ideal domain.
  • Test polynomials for irreducibility: roots, the rational root test, Eisenstein's criterion, reduction mod ppp.
  • Place a ring in the chain Euclidean domain ⊂ PID ⊂ UFD ⊂ integral domain, and show that Z[−5]\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]Z[−5​] is not a UFD.
  • Build C\mathbb{C}C as R[x]/(x2+1)\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)R[x]/(x2+1) and the finite fields F4\mathbb{F}_4F4​ and F8\mathbb{F}_8F8​, and compute in them.

Chapter 1 — Rings

Terminology

  • Ring — a set RRR with two operations +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ such that:
    1. (R,+)(R, +)(R,+) is an abelian group, with identity 000 and inverses −a-a−a;
    2. multiplication is associative: (ab)c=a(bc)(ab)c = a(bc)(ab)c=a(bc);
    3. there is a multiplicative identity 111 with 1a=a1=a1a = a1 = a1a=a1=a;
    4. the distributive laws hold: a(b+c)=ab+aca(b + c) = ab + aca(b+c)=ab+ac and (a+b)c=ac+bc(a + b)c = ac + bc(a+b)c=ac+bc.
  • Convention. In this series every ring has a 111 (some books call these "rings with unity" and allow rings without one). Multiplication need not be commutative.
  • Commutative ring — a ring with ab=baab = baab=ba for all a,ba, ba,b.
  • Zero ring — {0}\{0\}{0} with 1=01 = 01=0. It is the only ring in which 1=01 = 01=0 (if 1=01 = 01=0 then a=1a=0a=0a = 1a = 0a = 0a=1a=0a=0).
  • Unit — an element uuu with a two-sided inverse: uv=vu=1uv = vu = 1uv=vu=1. The units form a group R×R^\timesR× under multiplication.
  • Zero divisor — a nonzero aaa for which some nonzero bbb has ab=0ab = 0ab=0 or ba=0ba = 0ba=0.
  • Integral domain — a commutative ring with 1≠01 \ne 01=0 and no zero divisors.
  • Field — a commutative ring with 1≠01 \ne 01=0 in which every nonzero element is a unit.
  • Division ring — like a field but not necessarily commutative (the quaternions are the standard example).

First consequences of the axioms

For all a,ba, ba,b in a ring:

  1. 0⋅a=a⋅0=00 \cdot a = a \cdot 0 = 00⋅a=a⋅0=0. Proof: 0a=(0+0)a=0a+0a0a = (0 + 0)a = 0a + 0a0a=(0+0)a=0a+0a; subtract 0a0a0a from both sides.
  2. (−a)b=a(−b)=−(ab)(-a)b = a(-b) = -(ab)(−a)b=a(−b)=−(ab). Proof: ab+(−a)b=(a+(−a))b=0b=0ab + (-a)b = (a + (-a))b = 0b = 0ab+(−a)b=(a+(−a))b=0b=0.
  3. (−a)(−b)=ab(-a)(-b) = ab(−a)(−b)=ab, and in particular (−1)2=1(-1)^2 = 1(−1)2=1.

Cancellation. In an integral domain, if a≠0a \ne 0a=0 and ab=acab = acab=ac then b=cb = cb=c, because a(b−c)=0a(b - c) = 0a(b−c)=0 forces b−c=0b - c = 0b−c=0. This is exactly what fails in Z/12Z\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}Z/12Z: 2⋅1=2⋅72 \cdot 1 = 2 \cdot 72⋅1=2⋅7 but 1≠71 \ne 71=7.

Every field is an integral domain: if a≠0a \ne 0a=0 and ab=0ab = 0ab=0, then b=a−1ab=0b = a^{-1}ab = 0b=a−1ab=0. The converse fails (Z\mathbb{Z}Z), except for finite rings:

Theorem. A finite integral domain is a field.

Proof. Let RRR be a finite domain and a≠0a \ne 0a=0. The map μa:R→R\mu_a : R \to Rμa​:R→R, x↦axx \mapsto axx↦ax, is injective by cancellation. An injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective, so ax=1ax = 1ax=1 for some xxx. Since RRR is commutative, xxx is a two-sided inverse. ∎

Corollary. Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ is a field if and only if nnn is prime. (If n=abn = abn=ab with 1<a,b<n1 < a, b < n1<a,b<n, then aaa and bbb are zero divisors. If n=pn = pn=p is prime, Z/pZ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}Z/pZ has no zero divisors because p∣abp \mid abp∣ab implies p∣ap \mid ap∣a or p∣bp \mid bp∣b, post 00; so it is a finite domain.) This field is written Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​.

Characteristic

The characteristic of a ring RRR is the least n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 with n⋅1=1+1+⋯+1=0n \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 + \cdots + 1 = 0n⋅1=1+1+⋯+1=0 (nnn terms), or 000 if there is no such nnn. So char⁡Z=char⁡Q=0\operatorname{char}\mathbb{Z} = \operatorname{char}\mathbb{Q} = 0charZ=charQ=0 and char⁡Z/nZ=n\operatorname{char}\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} = ncharZ/nZ=n.

Theorem. The characteristic of an integral domain is 000 or a prime.

Proof. Suppose char⁡R=n>0\operatorname{char} R = n > 0charR=n>0 and n=abn = abn=ab with 1≤a,b<n1 \le a, b < n1≤a,b<n. Then 0=n⋅1=(a⋅1)(b⋅1)0 = n \cdot 1 = (a \cdot 1)(b \cdot 1)0=n⋅1=(a⋅1)(b⋅1). In a domain one factor is 000, contradicting the minimality of nnn. And n≠1n \ne 1n=1 because 1≠01 \ne 01=0. ∎

Watch out: characteristic is about n⋅1n \cdot 1n⋅1, not about the size of the ring. The infinite field Fp(t)\mathbb{F}_p(t)Fp​(t) of rational functions over Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ has characteristic ppp.

Chapter 2 — Homomorphisms, ideals and quotient rings

Terminology

  • Subring — a subset S⊆RS \subseteq RS⊆R containing 111 that is closed under +++, −-− and ⋅\cdot⋅. Example: Z⊂Z[i]⊂C\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Z}[i] \subset \mathbb{C}Z⊂Z[i]⊂C.
  • Ring homomorphism — a map φ:R→S\varphi : R \to Sφ:R→S with φ(a+b)=φ(a)+φ(b)\varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b)φ(a+b)=φ(a)+φ(b), φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b)\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) and φ(1)=1\varphi(1) = 1φ(1)=1.
  • Kernel — ker⁡φ={a:φ(a)=0}\ker\varphi = \{a : \varphi(a) = 0\}kerφ={a:φ(a)=0}.
  • Ideal — an additive subgroup I⊆RI \subseteq RI⊆R that absorbs multiplication: ra∈Ir a \in Ira∈I and ar∈Ia r \in Iar∈I for all r∈Rr \in Rr∈R, a∈Ia \in Ia∈I. (For commutative rings one condition suffices.)
  • Principal ideal — in a commutative ring, (a)=aR={ra:r∈R}(a) = aR = \{ra : r \in R\}(a)=aR={ra:r∈R}, the smallest ideal containing aaa. More generally (a1,…,ak)={r1a1+⋯+rkak}(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \{r_1a_1 + \cdots + r_ka_k\}(a1​,…,ak​)={r1​a1​+⋯+rk​ak​}.

Examples of homomorphisms: reduction Z→Z/nZ\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z→Z/nZ; evaluation R[x]→C\mathbb{R}[x] \to \mathbb{C}R[x]→C, f↦f(i)f \mapsto f(i)f↦f(i); complex conjugation C→C\mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}C→C; the inclusion of a subring.

Ideals are the kernels

Theorem. The kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal.

Proof. It is an additive subgroup, being the kernel of a homomorphism of additive groups (post 03). If φ(a)=0\varphi(a) = 0φ(a)=0 then φ(ra)=φ(r)⋅0=0\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r) \cdot 0 = 0φ(ra)=φ(r)⋅0=0 and φ(ar)=0\varphi(ar) = 0φ(ar)=0. ∎

Ideals are to rings what normal subgroups are to groups: exactly the things you can take a quotient by. Two quick facts:

  • If an ideal III contains a unit uuu, then I=RI = RI=R: for any rrr, r=(ru−1)u∈Ir = (ru^{-1})u \in Ir=(ru−1)u∈I. So a proper ideal contains no units, and in particular does not contain 111.
  • A commutative ring RRR with 1≠01 \ne 01=0 is a field if and only if its only ideals are {0}\{0\}{0} and RRR. (If RRR is a field, any nonzero ideal contains a unit. Conversely, for a≠0a \ne 0a=0, (a)=R∋1(a) = R \ni 1(a)=R∋1, so ra=1ra = 1ra=1 for some rrr.) Consequently every ring homomorphism from a field to a nonzero ring is injective: its kernel is a proper ideal (it misses 1), hence {0}\{0\}{0}.

Theorem. Every ideal of Z\mathbb{Z}Z is nZ=(n)n\mathbb{Z} = (n)nZ=(n) for a unique n≥0n \ge 0n≥0.

Proof. Let I≠{0}I \ne \{0\}I={0} and let nnn be the least positive element of III. For a∈Ia \in Ia∈I divide: a=qn+ra = qn + ra=qn+r with 0≤r<n0 \le r < n0≤r<n. Then r=a−qn∈Ir = a - qn \in Ir=a−qn∈I, so r=0r = 0r=0 by minimality, and a∈(n)a \in (n)a∈(n). ∎

In Z\mathbb{Z}Z, (a,b)=(gcd⁡(a,b))(a, b) = (\gcd(a, b))(a,b)=(gcd(a,b)): for example (4,6)=(2)(4, 6) = (2)(4,6)=(2). This is Bézout's identity from post 00 in ideal language.

Quotient rings

Let III be an ideal of RRR. The additive cosets a+Ia + Ia+I form an abelian group R/IR/IR/I (post 02). Define multiplication by (a+I)(b+I)=ab+I(a + I)(b + I) = ab + I(a+I)(b+I)=ab+I.

Well defined. If a′=a+ia' = a + ia′=a+i and b′=b+jb' = b + jb′=b+j with i,j∈Ii, j \in Ii,j∈I, then a′b′=ab+(aj+ib+ij)a'b' = ab + (aj + ib + ij)a′b′=ab+(aj+ib+ij), and the bracket lies in III because III absorbs multiplication. This is precisely where "ideal" (rather than just "subring") is needed. The ring axioms for R/IR/IR/I follow from those of RRR, with 1+I1 + I1+I as identity, and π:R→R/I\pi : R \to R/Iπ:R→R/I, a↦a+Ia \mapsto a + Ia↦a+I, is a surjective homomorphism with kernel III.

Theorem (First Isomorphism Theorem for rings). If φ:R→S\varphi : R \to Sφ:R→S is a ring homomorphism, then R/ker⁡φ≅im⁡φR/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphiR/kerφ≅imφ via a+ker⁡φ↦φ(a)a + \ker\varphi \mapsto \varphi(a)a+kerφ↦φ(a).

Proof. By the group version (post 03) the map φˉ\bar\varphiφˉ​ is a well-defined isomorphism of additive groups. It is multiplicative: φˉ((a+K)(b+K))=φˉ(ab+K)=φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b)\bar\varphi((a + K)(b + K)) = \bar\varphi(ab + K) = \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)φˉ​((a+K)(b+K))=φˉ​(ab+K)=φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b); and φˉ(1+K)=φ(1)=1\bar\varphi(1 + K) = \varphi(1) = 1φˉ​(1+K)=φ(1)=1. ∎

Worked applications:

  • Z[x]/(x)≅Z\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x) \cong \mathbb{Z}Z[x]/(x)≅Z. Evaluation at 0, f↦f(0)f \mapsto f(0)f↦f(0), is surjective, and its kernel is the polynomials with zero constant term, which is (x)(x)(x).
  • R[x]/(x2+1)≅C\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb{C}R[x]/(x2+1)≅C. Evaluation at iii is surjective (a+bx↦a+bia + bx \mapsto a + bia+bx↦a+bi). Its kernel contains x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1; Chapter 6 shows that (x2+1)(x^2 + 1)(x2+1) is a maximal ideal, so the kernel (a proper ideal containing it) is exactly (x2+1)(x^2 + 1)(x2+1).
  • Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z\mathbb{Z}[x]/(2, x) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z. The map f↦f(0) mod 2f \mapsto f(0) \bmod 2f↦f(0)mod2 is surjective with kernel {f:f(0) even}=(2,x)\{f : f(0) \text{ even}\} = (2, x){f:f(0) even}=(2,x).
  • Chinese Remainder Theorem. If gcd⁡(m,n)=1\gcd(m, n) = 1gcd(m,n)=1, the map Z→Z/m×Z/n\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/m \times \mathbb{Z}/nZ→Z/m×Z/n, a↦(a mod m,a mod n)a \mapsto (a \bmod m, a \bmod n)a↦(amodm,amodn), is a surjective ring homomorphism (surjective by post 00's CRT) with kernel (m)∩(n)=(mn)(m) \cap (n) = (mn)(m)∩(n)=(mn). So Z/mnZ≅Z/mZ×Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/mn\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/mnZ≅Z/mZ×Z/nZ as rings, and taking units gives ϕ(mn)=ϕ(m)ϕ(n)\phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n)ϕ(mn)=ϕ(m)ϕ(n) for Euler's function.

Trick: the fastest way to understand R/IR/IR/I is again to find a surjective homomorphism out of RRR whose kernel is III. Evaluation maps are the usual candidates for polynomial rings.

Chapter 3 — Prime and maximal ideals

From here on, "ring" means commutative ring with 111.

Terminology

  • Prime ideal — a proper ideal PPP such that ab∈Pab \in Pab∈P implies a∈Pa \in Pa∈P or b∈Pb \in Pb∈P.
  • Maximal ideal — a proper ideal MMM such that no ideal lies strictly between MMM and RRR: if M⊆J⊆RM \subseteq J \subseteq RM⊆J⊆R then J=MJ = MJ=M or J=RJ = RJ=R.

In Z\mathbb{Z}Z: (p)(p)(p) for a prime ppp is prime (this is Euclid's lemma) and maximal; (0)(0)(0) is prime (because Z\mathbb{Z}Z is a domain) but not maximal, since (0)⊊(2)⊊Z(0) \subsetneq (2) \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}(0)⊊(2)⊊Z; (6)(6)(6) is neither, since 2⋅3∈(6)2 \cdot 3 \in (6)2⋅3∈(6) but 2,3∉(6)2, 3 \notin (6)2,3∈/(6).

The two quotient theorems

Theorem. PPP is a prime ideal of RRR if and only if R/PR/PR/P is an integral domain.

Proof. R/PR/PR/P is not the zero ring exactly when 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P, i.e. when PPP is proper. In R/PR/PR/P, the product (a+P)(b+P)=ab+P(a + P)(b + P) = ab + P(a+P)(b+P)=ab+P is zero exactly when ab∈Pab \in Pab∈P, and a+Pa + Pa+P is zero exactly when a∈Pa \in Pa∈P. So "no zero divisors in R/PR/PR/P" says word for word "ab∈P⇒a∈Pab \in P \Rightarrow a \in Pab∈P⇒a∈P or b∈Pb \in Pb∈P". ∎

Theorem. MMM is a maximal ideal of RRR if and only if R/MR/MR/M is a field.

Proof. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Let a+M≠0a + M \ne 0a+M=0, i.e. a∉Ma \notin Ma∈/M. The ideal M+(a)={m+ra}M + (a) = \{m + ra\}M+(a)={m+ra} strictly contains MMM, so by maximality it is RRR and contains 111: 1=m+ra1 = m + ra1=m+ra for some m∈Mm \in Mm∈M, r∈Rr \in Rr∈R. Then (r+M)(a+M)=ra+M=1−m+M=1+M(r + M)(a + M) = ra + M = 1 - m + M = 1 + M(r+M)(a+M)=ra+M=1−m+M=1+M, so a+Ma + Ma+M is a unit. Also 1+M≠01 + M \ne 01+M=0 because MMM is proper.

(⇐\Leftarrow⇐) If R/MR/MR/M is a field, MMM is proper. Let M⊊JM \subsetneq JM⊊J and pick a∈J∖Ma \in J \setminus Ma∈J∖M. Then a+Ma + Ma+M has an inverse r+Mr + Mr+M, so ra−1∈M⊆Jra - 1 \in M \subseteq Jra−1∈M⊆J. Since ra∈Jra \in Jra∈J, also 1∈J1 \in J1∈J and J=RJ = RJ=R. ∎

Corollary. Every maximal ideal is prime (a field is a domain).

Examples in Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x].

  • (x)(x)(x) is prime but not maximal: Z[x]/(x)≅Z\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x) \cong \mathbb{Z}Z[x]/(x)≅Z is a domain but not a field. Indeed (x)⊊(2,x)⊊Z[x](x) \subsetneq (2, x) \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}[x](x)⊊(2,x)⊊Z[x].
  • (2,x)(2, x)(2,x) is maximal: Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z\mathbb{Z}[x]/(2, x) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z, a field.
  • (x2+1)(x^2 + 1)(x2+1) is prime but not maximal: Z[x]/(x2+1)≅Z[i]\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2+1) \cong \mathbb{Z}[i]Z[x]/(x2+1)≅Z[i], a domain that is not a field.

A standard existence result (it needs Zorn's lemma): every proper ideal of a ring with 111 is contained in a maximal ideal.

Chapter 4 — Polynomial rings over a field

Let FFF be a field. F[x]F[x]F[x] is the ring of polynomials a0+a1x+⋯+anxna_0 + a_1x + \cdots + a_nx^na0​+a1​x+⋯+an​xn with ai∈Fa_i \in Fai​∈F. If an≠0a_n \ne 0an​=0, the degree is nnn and ana_nan​ is the leading coefficient; the polynomial is monic if an=1a_n = 1an​=1. The zero polynomial has no degree (some books use −∞-\infty−∞).

Degree, units, roots

If RRR is a domain, the leading coefficient of fgfgfg is the product of the leading coefficients, which is nonzero. Hence, for nonzero f,gf, gf,g:

deg⁡(fg)=deg⁡f+deg⁡g,\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g, deg(fg)=degf+degg,

R[x]R[x]R[x] is again a domain, and the units of F[x]F[x]F[x] are the nonzero constants (a unit fff has deg⁡f+deg⁡f−1=0\deg f + \deg f^{-1} = 0degf+degf−1=0).

Theorem (division algorithm). For f,g∈F[x]f, g \in F[x]f,g∈F[x] with g≠0g \ne 0g=0 there are unique q,r∈F[x]q, r \in F[x]q,r∈F[x] with f=qg+rf = qg + rf=qg+r and either r=0r = 0r=0 or deg⁡r<deg⁡g\deg r < \deg gdegr<degg.

Proof sketch. Existence by induction on deg⁡f\deg fdegf: if deg⁡f≥deg⁡g=m\deg f \ge \deg g = mdegf≥degg=m, subtract (an/bm) xn−mg(a_n/b_m)\,x^{n-m}g(an​/bm​)xn−mg to kill the leading term of fff and apply induction to the result. Dividing by bmb_mbm​ is where a field is used. Uniqueness: if qg+r=q′g+r′qg + r = q'g + r'qg+r=q′g+r′ then (q−q′)g=r′−r(q - q')g = r' - r(q−q′)g=r′−r; the right side has degree <m< m<m, so q=q′q = q'q=q′ by the degree formula, and then r=r′r = r'r=r′. ∎

Worked example. Divide f=x4+3x3−2x+5f = x^4 + 3x^3 - 2x + 5f=x4+3x3−2x+5 by g=x2+x+1g = x^2 + x + 1g=x2+x+1 in Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x]:

x4+3x3−2x+5=(x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)+(8−x).x^4 + 3x^3 - 2x + 5 = (x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 + 2x - 3) + (8 - x). x4+3x3−2x+5=(x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)+(8−x).

(Check: (x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)=x4+3x3−x−3(x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 + 2x - 3) = x^4 + 3x^3 - x - 3(x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)=x4+3x3−x−3, and adding 8−x8 - x8−x gives fff.)

Factor theorem. aaa is a root of fff if and only if (x−a)∣f(x - a) \mid f(x−a)∣f (divide by x−ax - ax−a; the remainder is the constant f(a)f(a)f(a)). So a nonzero polynomial of degree nnn over a domain has at most nnn roots.

Common pitfall: over a ring with zero divisors this fails. In Z/8Z\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}Z/8Z, x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1 has four roots: 1,3,5,71, 3, 5, 71,3,5,7 (each squares to 111 mod 8).

F[x] is a principal ideal domain

A principal ideal domain (PID) is an integral domain in which every ideal is principal.

Theorem. If FFF is a field, F[x]F[x]F[x] is a PID.

Proof. Let I≠{0}I \ne \{0\}I={0} be an ideal and let g∈Ig \in Ig∈I be nonzero of least degree. For f∈If \in If∈I write f=qg+rf = qg + rf=qg+r. Then r=f−qg∈Ir = f - qg \in Ir=f−qg∈I and, if r≠0r \ne 0r=0, deg⁡r<deg⁡g\deg r < \deg gdegr<degg, contradicting minimality. So r=0r = 0r=0 and I=(g)I = (g)I=(g). ∎

The proof is the one for Z\mathbb{Z}Z with "size" replaced by "degree". As in Z\mathbb{Z}Z, (f,g)=(gcd⁡(f,g))(f, g) = (\gcd(f, g))(f,g)=(gcd(f,g)), and the Euclidean algorithm computes the gcd:

x6−1=x2 (x4−1)+(x2−1),x4−1=(x2+1)(x2−1)+0,\begin{aligned} x^6 - 1 &= x^2\,(x^4 - 1) + (x^2 - 1), \\ x^4 - 1 &= (x^2 + 1)(x^2 - 1) + 0, \end{aligned} x6−1x4−1​=x2(x4−1)+(x2−1),=(x2+1)(x2−1)+0,​

so gcd⁡(x6−1,x4−1)=x2−1\gcd(x^6 - 1, x^4 - 1) = x^2 - 1gcd(x6−1,x4−1)=x2−1.

Watch out: Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x] is not a PID, although Z\mathbb{Z}Z is. Suppose (2,x)=(h)(2, x) = (h)(2,x)=(h). Then h∣2h \mid 2h∣2, so hhh is a constant ±1\pm 1±1 or ±2\pm 2±2. h=±1h = \pm 1h=±1 is impossible because (2,x)(2, x)(2,x) is proper (its quotient is Z/2\mathbb{Z}/2Z/2). h=±2h = \pm 2h=±2 is impossible because x∉(2)x \notin (2)x∈/(2).

Irreducibility tests

A nonzero non-unit f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x] is irreducible if it is not a product of two polynomials of smaller degree. Irreducible polynomials are the "primes" of F[x]F[x]F[x], and whether fff is irreducible depends on the field: x2−2x^2 - 2x2−2 is irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q but factors as (x−2)(x+2)(x - \sqrt2)(x + \sqrt2)(x−2​)(x+2​) over R\mathbb{R}R; x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 is irreducible over R\mathbb{R}R but not over C\mathbb{C}C.

  1. Degree 2 or 3. A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is irreducible if and only if it has no root in the field (any factorisation includes a linear factor).
  2. Rational root test. If f=anxn+⋯+a0∈Z[x]f = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_0 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]f=an​xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[x] and p/qp/qp/q in lowest terms is a root, then p∣a0p \mid a_0p∣a0​ and q∣anq \mid a_nq∣an​.
  3. Gauss's lemma. A polynomial in Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x] that factors in Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x] into factors of lower degree already factors in Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x] into factors of those same degrees. So it suffices to look for integer factorisations.
  4. Eisenstein's criterion. Let f=anxn+⋯+a0∈Z[x]f = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_0 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]f=an​xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[x] and ppp a prime with p∤anp \nmid a_np∤an​, p∣aip \mid a_ip∣ai​ for all i<ni < ni<n, and p2∤a0p^2 \nmid a_0p2∤a0​. Then fff is irreducible in Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x].
  5. Reduction mod ppp. Let f∈Z[x]f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]f∈Z[x] and let ppp be a prime not dividing the leading coefficient. If the reduction fˉ∈Fp[x]\bar f \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]fˉ​∈Fp​[x] is irreducible (of the same degree), then fff is irreducible in Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x].

Worked examples:

  • x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2: Eisenstein with p=2p = 2p=2. Also, the rational root test leaves only ±1,±2\pm 1, \pm 2±1,±2, none of which is a root.
  • x3+2x+1x^3 + 2x + 1x3+2x+1: candidates ±1\pm 1±1 give 444 and −2-2−2, so no rational root; degree 3, so irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q.
  • x5−4x+2x^5 - 4x + 2x5−4x+2: Eisenstein with p=2p = 2p=2 (2∣−42 \mid -42∣−4, 2∣22 \mid 22∣2, 4∤24 \nmid 24∤2). This polynomial returns in post 05.
  • Cyclotomic polynomial Φ5(x)=x4+x3+x2+x+1=(x5−1)/(x−1)\Phi_5(x) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = (x^5 - 1)/(x - 1)Φ5​(x)=x4+x3+x2+x+1=(x5−1)/(x−1). Eisenstein does not apply directly, but f(x)f(x)f(x) is irreducible exactly when f(x+1)f(x+1)f(x+1) is, and
    Φ5(x+1)=x4+5x3+10x2+10x+5\Phi_5(x + 1) = x^4 + 5x^3 + 10x^2 + 10x + 5Φ5​(x+1)=x4+5x3+10x2+10x+5, which is Eisenstein at 555.
  • x4+5x3+3x2+7x+11x^4 + 5x^3 + 3x^2 + 7x + 11x4+5x3+3x2+7x+11: reduce mod 2 to x4+x3+x2+x+1x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1x4+x3+x2+x+1, which is irreducible in F2[x]\mathbb{F}_2[x]F2​[x]. So the original is irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

Common pitfall: "no rational roots" proves irreducibility only in degree 2 and 3. x4+4x^4 + 4x4+4 has no rational root, yet x4+4=(x2+2x+2)(x2−2x+2)x^4 + 4 = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2)x4+4=(x2+2x+2)(x2−2x+2).

Common pitfall: the reduction test only works one way. x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 is irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, but mod 2 it is (x+1)2(x + 1)^2(x+1)2. A reducible reduction proves nothing; so does a failed Eisenstein check.

Chapter 5 — Unique factorisation

Terminology

In an integral domain RRR:

  • aaa divides bbb, written a∣ba \mid ba∣b, if b=acb = acb=ac for some c∈Rc \in Rc∈R.
  • aaa and bbb are associates if a=uba = uba=ub for a unit uuu (for example 222 and −2-2−2 in Z\mathbb{Z}Z, or 1+i1 + i1+i and i(1+i)=−1+ii(1+i) = -1 + ii(1+i)=−1+i in Z[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]Z[i]).
  • A nonzero non-unit ppp is irreducible if p=abp = abp=ab forces aaa or bbb to be a unit.
  • A nonzero non-unit ppp is prime if p∣abp \mid abp∣ab forces p∣ap \mid ap∣a or p∣bp \mid bp∣b (equivalently, (p)(p)(p) is a prime ideal).
  • Unique factorisation domain (UFD) — a domain in which every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and associates.
  • Euclidean domain — a domain with a function N:R∖{0}→Z≥0N : R \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}N:R∖{0}→Z≥0​ such that for all aaa and b≠0b \ne 0b=0 there are q,rq, rq,r with a=qb+ra = qb + ra=qb+r and r=0r = 0r=0 or N(r)<N(b)N(r) < N(b)N(r)<N(b).

Prime implies irreducible in any domain: if ppp is prime and p=abp = abp=ab, then p∣abp \mid abp∣ab, say p∣ap \mid ap∣a, so a=pca = pca=pc and p=pcbp = pcbp=pcb; cancelling gives cb=1cb = 1cb=1, so bbb is a unit. The converse holds in a UFD (and so in a PID) but fails in general, which is exactly how unique factorisation breaks.

The hierarchy

fields⊂Euclidean domains⊂PIDs⊂UFDs⊂integral domains.\text{fields} \subset \text{Euclidean domains} \subset \text{PIDs} \subset \text{UFDs} \subset \text{integral domains}. fields⊂Euclidean domains⊂PIDs⊂UFDs⊂integral domains.

  • Euclidean ⇒ PID: the proof that F[x]F[x]F[x] is a PID works verbatim with NNN in place of degree.
  • PID ⇒ UFD: a standard theorem (existence uses the fact that increasing chains of ideals in a PID stop; uniqueness uses "irreducible ⇒ prime" in a PID).
  • Every inclusion is strict, as the diagram's examples show.

A domain without unique factorisation

Let R=Z[−5]={a+b−5:a,b∈Z}R = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}R=Z[−5​]={a+b−5​:a,b∈Z} with norm N(a+b−5)=a2+5b2N(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2N(a+b−5​)=a2+5b2, again multiplicative. In RRR,

Practice Exercises

1. List the units and the zero divisors of Z/15Z\mathbb{Z}/15\mathbb{Z}Z/15Z.

Solution

Units are the classes coprime to 15: 1,2,4,7,8,11,13,141, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 141,2,4,7,8,11,13,14 (there are ϕ(15)=8\phi(15) = 8ϕ(15)=8). The other nonzero classes, 3,5,6,9,10,123, 5, 6, 9, 10, 123,5,6,9,10,12, are zero divisors: for example 3⋅5=15≡03 \cdot 5 = 15 \equiv 03⋅5=15≡0 and 6⋅5=30≡06 \cdot 5 = 30 \equiv 06⋅5=30≡0.

2. Show that (x)(x)(x) is a prime ideal of Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x] that is also maximal, while in Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x] it is prime but not maximal. What changes?

Solution

Evaluation at 0 gives Q[x]/(x)≅Q\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x) \cong \mathbb{Q}Q[x]/(x)≅Q, a field, so (x)(x)(x) is maximal in Q[x]\mathbb{Q}[x]Q[x]. The same map gives Z[x]/(x)≅Z\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x) \cong \mathbb{Z}Z[x]/(x)≅Z, a domain but not a field, so (x)(x)(x) is prime but not maximal in Z[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]Z[x]; indeed (x)⊊(2,x)(x) \subsetneq (2, x)(x)⊊(2,x). What changed is the coefficient ring: the quotient is the coefficient ring itself.

3. Decide whether x3+2x+1x^3 + 2x + 1x3+2x+1 is irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q and over F3\mathbb{F}_3F3​.

Solution

Over Q\mathbb{Q}Q: the rational root test leaves ±1\pm 1±1, giving values 444 and −2-2−2; no root, degree 3, so irreducible. Over F3\mathbb{F}_3F3​: f(0)=1f(0) = 1f(0)=1, f(1)=4≡1f(1) = 4 \equiv 1f(1)=4≡1, f(2)=13≡1f(2) = 13 \equiv 1f(2)=13≡1; no root, so irreducible, and F3[x]/(x3+2x+1)\mathbb{F}_3[x]/(x^3 + 2x + 1)F3​[x]/(x3+2x+1) is a field with 272727 elements.

4. Use Eisenstein's criterion to show x4+10x+5x^4 + 10x + 5x4+10x+5 is irreducible over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. Why does "it has no rational root" not suffice on its own?

Solution

With p=5p = 5p=5: 5∤15 \nmid 15∤1 (leading coefficient), 555 divides 0,0,10,50, 0, 10, 50,0,10,5, and 25∤525 \nmid 525∤5. So it is irreducible. Absence of roots only rules out linear factors; a quartic could still split into two quadratics, as x4+4x^4 + 4x4+4 does.

5. In F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1)\mathbb{F}_4 = \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2 + x + 1)F4​=F2​[x]/(x2+x+1), compute α3\alpha^3α3, (α+1)2(\alpha + 1)^2(α+1)2 and α−1\alpha^{-1}α−1.

6. Show that 333 is irreducible but not prime in Z[−5]\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]Z[−5​], using 9=(2+−5)(2−−5)9 = (2 + \sqrt{-5})(2 - \sqrt{-5})9=(2+−5​)(2−−5​).

Solution

N(3)=9N(3) = 9N(3)=9. A proper factor would have norm 3, and a2+5b2=3a^2 + 5b^2 = 3a2+5b2=3 has no integer solution, so 333 is irreducible. Next, (2+−5)(2−−5)=4+5=9(2 + \sqrt{-5})(2 - \sqrt{-5}) = 4 + 5 = 9(2+−5​)(2−−5​)=4+5=9, so 333 divides this product. But 333 divides neither factor, since (2±−5)/3∉Z[−5](2 \pm \sqrt{-5})/3 \notin \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}](2±−5​)/3∈/Z[−5​]. So 333 is not prime.

7. Show that Z[i]/(2+i)≅Z/5Z\mathbb{Z}[i]/(2 + i) \cong \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}Z[i]/(2+i)≅Z/5Z.

Solution

Let ψ:Z→Z[i]/(2+i)\psi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}[i]/(2 + i)ψ:Z→Z[i]/(2+i) be the natural map. It is surjective: i≡−2i \equiv -2i≡−2 modulo (2+i)(2 + i)(2+i), so a+bi≡a−2ba + bi \equiv a - 2ba+bi≡a−2b, an integer. Its kernel contains 5=(2+i)(2−i)5 = (2 + i)(2 - i)5=(2+i)(2−i). If an integer nnn lies in (2+i)(2 + i)(2+i), then n=(2+i)γn = (2 + i)\gamman=(2+i)γ and n2=N(n)=5N(γ)n^2 = N(n) = 5N(\gamma)n2=N(n)=5N(γ), so 5∣n25 \mid n^25∣n2 and 5∣n5 \mid n5∣n. So the kernel is 5Z5\mathbb{Z}5Z, and the First Isomorphism Theorem gives Z/5Z≅Z[i]/(2+i)\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}[i]/(2 + i)Z/5Z≅Z[i]/(2+i).

What's next

Post 05 turns the construction of Chapter 6 into a theory. If ppp is irreducible over FFF, the field F[x]/(p)F[x]/(p)F[x]/(p) contains a root of ppp, so it is an extension of FFF of degree deg⁡p\deg pdegp. Degrees multiply in towers, which already settles the Greek problems of doubling the cube and trisecting an angle. Adding all the roots of a polynomial gives its splitting field, and the automorphisms of that field form its Galois group. The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory matches subfields with subgroups, and it explains why there is no formula in radicals for the roots of a general quintic.

References

  • D. S. Dummit and R. M. Foote, Abstract Algebra, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2004 — Chapters 7 (rings, ideals, quotients), 8 (Euclidean domains, PIDs, UFDs; the example Z[(1+−19)/2]\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-19})/2]Z[(1+−19​)/2]) and 9 (polynomial rings, irreducibility criteria).
  • M. Artin, Algebra, 2nd edition, Pearson, 2011 — Chapters 11 (rings) and 12 (factoring, Gauss's lemma, Gaussian integers).
  • J. A. Gallian, Contemporary Abstract Algebra, 10th edition, CRC Press, 2021 — rings, integral domains, ideals and factor rings, divisibility in integral domains.
  • T. W. Hungerford, Algebra, Springer GTM 73, 1974 — Chapter III for a more formal treatment (rings without 1, Zorn's lemma for maximal ideals).
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.702 Algebra II (Spring 2011) — lecture notes on rings, factoring and finite fields.
  • K. Conrad, Expository papers ("blurbs") — short notes on ring theory, Eisenstein's criterion and finite fields.
